items.title: L13: Applying FOI exemptions to government information
items.source: Freedom of Information Act 2000 (sections 12, 21, 22, 35, 36, 40, 41, 43); Information Commissioner's Office guidance on FOI exemptions
items.body: Under the Freedom of Information Act 2000 anyone can ask a public authority for recorded information, and the authority must normally respond within twenty working days. Information must be released unless an exemption applies. Some exemptions are absolute, meaning there is no public interest balancing. Section 40 covers personal data where disclosure would breach data protection principles, and section 41 covers information given in confidence where disclosure would be an actionable breach of confidence. Others are qualified, so the authority must weigh the public interest in withholding against the public interest in disclosure. Section 35 covers the formulation or development of government policy, ministerial communications and the operation of ministers' private offices; the safe space argument is that officials and ministers need room for frank discussion while policy is live, but its weight fades once a decision is taken. Section 36 covers prejudice to the effective conduct of public affairs, and a government department needs the reasonable opinion of a qualified person, normally a minister, before relying on it. Section 43 covers commercial interests, including those of a third party, where disclosure would or would be likely to prejudice them. Section 22 allows withholding of information intended for future publication, and section 21 covers information already reasonably accessible. Section 12 lets an authority refuse a request if finding the information would exceed the cost limit, which for central government is £600, though it should first offer advice on narrowing the request. Section 14 allows refusal of vexatious requests. A refusal notice must say which exemption applies and, for qualified exemptions, explain the public interest reasoning. A requester can ask for an internal review, then complain to the Information Commissioner, and appeal to the First-tier Tribunal.

questions.prompt: A request asks for minutes of a meeting where policy options were discussed, and the policy is still being developed. Which exemption is the department most likely to consider first?

options.text: Section 40, personal data, which is absolute and protects all minutes of meetings
Section 35, formulation of government policy, which is qualified
Section 12, the cost limit, which applies to any request involving a meeting
Section 21, information the requester can already reach by other means

questions.hint: Live policy discussion falls under section 35, subject to the public interest test.

questions.prompt: A department wants to rely on section 36 to withhold advice to ministers. What must happen before it can do so?

options.text: A qualified person, usually a minister, gives a reasonable opinion
The Information Commissioner approves the use of the exemption before it is applied
The requester is told the exemption applies before the request is logged
The Cabinet Secretary certifies that the information is exempt in each case

questions.hint: Section 36 needs the qualified person's reasonable opinion.

questions.prompt: A policy decision was announced six months ago and a request asks for the advice behind it. How does that affect a section 35 argument?

options.text: Section 35 can no longer be used at all once a decision has been announced publicly
The argument grows stronger, because advice should stay private after any decision is taken
Nothing changes, because policy advice is exempt for a fixed period of twenty years
The safe space argument weakens once the decision is taken

questions.hint: The weight of the safe space argument fades after a decision.

questions.prompt: Which pair of sections are both absolute exemptions, needing no public interest balancing?

options.text: Section 35 (policy) and section 36 (public affairs), since both protect ministers
Section 43 (commercial interests) and section 22 (future publication), since both concern timing
Section 40 (third-party personal data) and section 41 (information given in confidence)
Section 12 (cost) and section 14 (vexatious requests), since neither needs a test

questions.hint: Sections 40 and 41 are absolute; policy, public affairs and commercial interests are qualified.

questions.prompt: A request would take about forty hours to answer, which exceeds the cost limit. What does good practice require?

options.text: Refuse under section 12 but offer advice on how the request could be narrowed
Answer in full regardless, since the cost limit is only guidance for large requests
Refuse without comment, since the department has no duty to advise requesters
Release a first batch of documents and ignore the rest without explanation

questions.hint: Section 12 permits refusal but authorities should advise and assist.

questions.prompt: A request is for a supplier's pricing in a contract that is still being negotiated. Which exemption is relevant, and how is it treated?

options.text: Section 41, confidence, which is a qualified exemption needing a balancing test
Section 22, future publication, which is absolute where the contract is not yet signed
Section 43, commercial interests, a qualified exemption needing a public interest test
Section 14, vexatious requests, which applies whenever negotiations are live

questions.hint: Commercial interests are protected by section 43, subject to the public interest.

questions.prompt: A requester disagrees with the department's refusal. What is the usual route of challenge?

options.text: A complaint to the Parliamentary Ombudsman, then an appeal to the Cabinet Office
An appeal to the minister, then a referral to the National Audit Office
A request to the Speaker, then an inquiry by the Public Accounts Committee
Internal review, then the Information Commissioner, then the First-tier Tribunal

questions.hint: The FOI complaint route is internal review, ICO, then Tribunal.

questions.prompt: A department takes thirty-five working days to answer a straightforward FOI request without explanation. What is the position?

options.text: It is within time, since the clock stops while the department locates the information
It has missed the usual twenty working day limit without a valid extension
It is within time, since thirty working days is the normal period for central government
It has missed the limit, but only requests from MPs or journalists carry a deadline

questions.hint: The usual limit is twenty working days.

items.title: L13: Sharing data between departments lawfully
items.source: UK GDPR and Data Protection Act 2018; ICO Data Sharing Code of Practice; Digital Economy Act 2017 (public service delivery, debt and fraud powers)
items.body: Departments often need to share personal data, for example to check eligibility for a benefit or to tackle fraud. The UK GDPR and the Data Protection Act 2018 apply to government like any other organisation. The core principles are lawfulness, fairness and transparency, purpose limitation, data minimisation, accuracy, storage limitation, integrity and confidentiality, and accountability. Purpose limitation means data collected for one purpose should not be used for an incompatible one without a proper basis. Data minimisation means sharing only what is necessary. Before sharing, the organisation must identify a lawful basis, which for public bodies is often that processing is necessary for a task carried out in the public interest or in the exercise of official authority, and, for special category data such as health, an additional condition. Where processing is likely to result in a high risk to people, a data protection impact assessment is required before it begins. Good practice is a written data sharing agreement setting out the purpose, the data, who is controller, security arrangements, retention and what happens if there is a breach. The ICO's Data Sharing Code explains how to do this. The Digital Economy Act 2017 gives powers for specified public authorities to share data for specified purposes, such as improving public services, tackling debt and fraud, and research, subject to codes of practice and safeguards. People have rights, including to be informed and to access their data, and breaches likely to cause risk to individuals must be reported to the ICO within seventy-two hours. Officials should involve the data protection officer early, since fixing a data flow after it has begun is much harder.

questions.prompt: A team wants to share a whole benefits dataset with another department to check one narrow category of claimant. Which principle is most directly engaged?

options.text: Storage limitation, so the data must be deleted within a week of sharing
Accuracy, so the Treasury must check the dataset before it is shared
Data minimisation, so only the data needed for the check should be shared
Lawfulness, since departments cannot share data with each other in any circumstances

questions.hint: Sharing everything when only part is needed breaches minimisation.

questions.prompt: A proposal involves large-scale use of health records for a new purpose. What is normally required before it starts?

options.text: A debate and vote in Parliament, since sharing health data always needs one
Approval from the Comptroller and Auditor General before any new data flow
The consent of every individual, which is the only lawful basis for health data
A data protection impact assessment, as the processing is high risk

questions.hint: High-risk processing requires a DPIA before it begins.

questions.prompt: Data collected to administer a licence is wanted by another team to target marketing for an unrelated scheme. What is the main issue?

options.text: Accuracy, because licence data is likely to be out of date for marketing
Purpose limitation, since the new use may be incompatible
Storage limitation, because licence records should be destroyed once a licence ends
Integrity, because the marketing team may lack the right security clearance

questions.hint: Using data for an incompatible new purpose engages purpose limitation.

questions.prompt: What is the value of a written data sharing agreement?

options.text: It records purpose, data, responsibilities, security and retention, so everyone knows what is agreed
It replaces the need for a lawful basis, since both departments have signed it
It makes the sharing exempt from the ICO's enforcement powers while it is in force
It moves all legal responsibility to the receiving department once data is sent

questions.hint: Agreements support clarity and accountability but do not replace a lawful basis.

questions.prompt: A department finds that personal data sent to a supplier was exposed, creating a risk to individuals. By when should the ICO normally be told?

options.text: Within thirty working days, in line with FOI requests
Within seventy-two hours of becoming aware of the breach
At the end of the financial year, in the annual report and accounts
Only after the affected individuals have complained to the ICO

questions.hint: Reportable breaches go to the ICO without undue delay, normally within seventy-two hours.

questions.prompt: What does the Digital Economy Act 2017 do for data sharing?

options.text: It lets any public body share any personal data with any other, for any purpose
It removes the data protection principles from government data sharing
It gives specified public authorities powers to share data for stated purposes, with codes and safeguards
It requires departments to publish personal data on request from the public

questions.hint: The Act creates specific powers with safeguards, not unlimited sharing.

questions.prompt: Which statement about sharing health data, which is special category data, is correct?

options.text: Public authorities need no lawful basis, because they hold data by right
A lawful basis is enough, with no further condition for health data
Only the individual's consent can ever be used for special category data
An extra condition is needed as well as a lawful basis

questions.hint: Special category data needs both a lawful basis and an additional condition.

questions.prompt: When should the data protection officer be consulted about a new data flow?

options.text: Early in the design, because changing a data flow once it is running is much harder
After the first transfer, so the DPO can review a real example
Only when an individual complains about how their data was used
Only if the data is classified SECRET or above

questions.hint: Early involvement avoids costly changes later.

items.title: L13: Public procurement principles in practice
items.source: Cabinet Office, Procurement Policy Notes and Sourcing Playbook; Procurement Act 2023 (principles of value for money, transparency, integrity, non-discrimination)
items.body: Government buys goods and services from the private and voluntary sectors, and the rules aim to deliver value for money while treating suppliers fairly. Public procurement law, now mainly the Procurement Act 2023, is built on principles of transparency, equal treatment and non-discrimination, proportionality and integrity, and requires contracting authorities to consider value for money and to avoid or manage conflicts of interest. In practice, competition is the default: opportunities above set thresholds are advertised publicly on the government's Find a Tender and Contracts Finder services, and the evaluation criteria and weightings are published in advance so that every bidder knows how it will be assessed. Bids are scored against those criteria by people who have declared that they have no conflicts, and the contract is awarded on the basis of the most advantageous tender, which considers quality as well as price. Direct awards without competition are allowed only in limited circumstances, such as extreme urgency or where only one supplier can provide the goods or services, and the reason should be recorded and justified, usually in a published notice. Contracts should be managed after award, with performance monitored and variations controlled, because large changes to a contract after award can amount to an unlawful new award. Officials involved in a procurement must keep discussions with suppliers fair: they should not give one bidder information that others lack, should avoid informal contacts during a live process, and should keep an audit trail. Suppliers can challenge unfair awards, and the courts can set aside contracts or award damages.

questions.prompt: During a live competition, a bidder's account manager asks an official informally how the evaluation is going. What should the official do?

options.text: Decline, and route questions through the formal process open to all bidders
Give a general indication, since a hint about progress gives no real advantage
Share the scoring weights so that the bidder can price more competitively
Arrange a private meeting so the supplier feels it was treated courteously

questions.hint: Fair treatment means all bidders get the same information through formal channels.

questions.prompt: A team wants to award a contract directly to one supplier because it has worked well with them before. What is the position?

options.text: It is allowed whenever the supplier has delivered well for the department before
It is allowed if the price is below the average of recent comparable contracts
Direct award is allowed only in limited circumstances, which must be recorded
It is allowed once a minister has signed off the choice of supplier

questions.hint: Competition is the default and direct awards need a recognised justification.

questions.prompt: Why are evaluation criteria and weightings published before bids are submitted?

options.text: So that suppliers can negotiate the weightings before they submit their bids
So that the department can adjust the weightings once it has seen the prices
So that the winner can be selected before the scoring begins
So bidders know how they will be assessed and the process is fair

questions.hint: Transparency lets bidders compete on equal terms.

questions.prompt: An evaluator realises that their brother-in-law works for one of the bidders. What should they do?

options.text: Say nothing, since an in-law is not close enough to count as a conflict
Declare it at once so the procurement lead can decide how to manage it, which may mean stepping aside
Score that bidder more strictly than the rest, to offset any suggestion of bias
Carry on scoring and add a private note that they felt uneasy about it

questions.hint: Conflicts must be declared and managed before they taint the process.

questions.prompt: A contract has been awarded, and the supplier now proposes a large change that effectively alters its scope. What is the risk?

options.text: There is no risk, since variations are always allowed once a contract is signed
A large change after award can amount to an unlawful new award that should have been competed
The Treasury will pay for the extra work, so there is no procurement issue
The change is void only if another supplier objects within a year

questions.hint: Large modifications may need a new competition.

questions.prompt: In an award based on the most advantageous tender, which bid wins?

options.text: The bid with the lowest price, whatever the quality of what is offered
The bid from the supplier with the longest record of working for government
The bid best overall against the published criteria, not the cheapest
The first compliant bid received after the competition opens

questions.hint: Quality and price are assessed against criteria.

questions.prompt: Which of these would normally support a decision to use a direct award?

options.text: A preference for a supplier the team already knows and trusts
A wish to avoid the effort of preparing competition documents
A supplier's request for an exclusive arrangement in return for a discount
Extreme urgency that the department did not cause

questions.hint: Genuine urgency or a single possible supplier can justify direct award.

questions.prompt: Why must an audit trail be kept for a procurement?

options.text: So decisions can be justified if a supplier challenges the award or the NAO reviews it
So that unsuccessful suppliers can see each other's scores in full
So that the minister can approve the winner after the contract is signed
So that records can be destroyed once the contract has been signed

questions.hint: Records show the process was fair and lawful.

items.title: L13: Consultation: the Gunning principles
items.source: Cabinet Office, Consultation Principles 2018; R v Brent LBC ex parte Gunning [1985]; R (Moseley) v Haringey LBC [2014] UKSC 56
items.body: Government consults people and organisations before taking decisions that affect them. There is often no general legal duty to consult, but one can arise from a statute, from a promise to consult, from past practice, or from fairness where a decision seriously affects people. When a department does consult, the courts expect it to be done properly. The Gunning principles, set out in a 1985 case and later approved by the Supreme Court, say that consultation must take place when proposals are still at a formative stage, so that the decision is not already made. The consultation must give sufficient reasons and information for those consulted to give intelligent consideration and a response. It must allow adequate time for people to respond, depending on the issue. And the decision-maker must conscientiously take into account the product of the consultation before deciding. The government's Consultation Principles say that consultation should be clear and concise, of a proportionate length and targeted at those who are affected, and that departments should consider whether they need to consult at all. They no longer set a fixed minimum period, though twelve weeks was the previous norm, and shorter or longer periods can be justified. The department should publish a response that explains what it heard and how it influenced the decision. Officials should also think about accessibility, such as easy read formats, and should consider the Public Sector Equality Duty. A consultation that is a mere formality, or that presents the decision as already made, risks challenge by judicial review and the decision may be quashed.

questions.prompt: A consultation document says the policy 'will be introduced next April' and asks only how best to implement it. What is the main risk?

options.text: It may breach the rule that every consultation must run for twelve weeks
It may breach the principle that proposals be at a formative stage
It may breach the rule that ministers must not take part in a consultation
It may breach the rule that consultations must be run by the Cabinet Office

questions.hint: A decision already made cannot be genuinely consulted on.

questions.prompt: A consultation withholds a key financial assessment, so respondents cannot judge the proposal. Which Gunning principle is most clearly breached?

options.text: Adequate time must be given for responses to be prepared
Responses must be conscientiously taken into account
Sufficient information for intelligent consideration
Proposals must be at a formative stage

questions.hint: Withholding material information undermines intelligent consideration.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly reflects the current Consultation Principles on the length of a consultation?

options.text: Every consultation must run for exactly twelve weeks, whatever its subject
Consultations should never run for longer than four weeks, to avoid delay
Consultations must stay open until the minister is satisfied with the responses
There is no fixed minimum; the length should be proportionate

questions.hint: The Principles say length should be proportionate.

questions.prompt: After a consultation closes, the minister decides without reading the responses, relying on a short note. Which principle is breached?

options.text: Conscientious consideration of the product of the consultation
Adequate time for responses to be prepared and sent in
Sufficient information for respondents to understand the proposal
The requirement that proposals be at a formative stage

questions.hint: The decision-maker must genuinely take responses into account.

questions.prompt: What should a department do after it closes a consultation?

options.text: Destroy the individual responses so that respondents' views stay confidential
Send the responses to the opposition so they can review the policy
Publish a response explaining what it heard and how that affected the decision
Wait for the NAO to analyse the responses before any decision is taken

questions.hint: Government should publish a response.

questions.prompt: A department has no statutory duty to consult on a change but has told stakeholders it will. What is the position?

options.text: Only an Act of Parliament can create a duty to consult, so none arises
A duty arises only if the National Audit Office recommends consultation
A duty arises only if a minister signs a formal commitment
A promise to consult can create an expectation to be honoured

questions.hint: A promise or past practice can create an expectation of consultation.

questions.prompt: Which action best supports accessible consultation?

options.text: Publishing only on the department's internal system, to keep responses controlled
Offering easy read and other formats so that affected groups can take part
Limiting responses to organisations that have registered with the department
Closing the consultation within a week to avoid delaying the policy

questions.hint: Accessibility widens participation and supports the equality duty.

questions.prompt: A court finds a consultation was a mere formality and the decision unlawful. What might the remedy be?

options.text: The decision may be quashed and consultation redone
The minister must resign under the Ministerial Code
The responses are laid before Parliament and the decision stands
The consultation is treated as complete if it ran for four weeks

questions.hint: A flawed consultation can lead to a quashing order.

items.title: L13: Appraising options: the Green Book and the five case model
items.source: HM Treasury, The Green Book: Central Government Guidance on Appraisal and Evaluation; Better Business Cases guidance
items.body: The Green Book is HM Treasury's guidance on how to appraise policies, programmes and projects, and how to evaluate them afterwards, so that public money is spent well. It applies across central government. Appraisal compares options by their costs, benefits and risks to society as a whole, not just to the government, and is expected before significant spending is agreed. A business case is built on the five case model. The strategic case sets out the case for change and fit with objectives. The economic case compares options and shows which offers best value for money to society. The commercial case considers whether a viable deal can be struck with suppliers. The financial case looks at affordability and funding. The management case covers whether the proposal can be delivered, including governance, risk and benefits realisation. Appraisal always includes a baseline, sometimes called the do-nothing or do-minimum, against which options are compared, and a short list of options that includes realistic alternatives. Costs and benefits that occur at different times are converted to present values by discounting, so that they can be compared, and results are tested through sensitivity analysis. Optimism bias is the tendency for project planners to be too optimistic about costs, timescales and benefits, and the guidance requires adjustments for it. Distributional effects and wider impacts, including on different groups and places, should be considered. Business cases are approved at stages, from an outline through to a full case, and are updated as plans become firmer. Good appraisal makes the decision-maker's reasoning visible and can be scrutinised by the Treasury, the NAO and Parliament.

questions.prompt: A business case compares three options but includes no baseline of what happens if nothing is done. What is the weakness?

options.text: The case lacks a strategic section, so the economic case cannot be completed
There is no reference point against which to measure each option
The case cannot be discounted unless it first assumes a baseline of zero cost
The Treasury will assume the cheapest option is best by default

questions.hint: Appraisal needs a baseline for comparison.

questions.prompt: Which of the five cases looks at affordability and funding?

options.text: The commercial case
The economic case
The financial case
The management case

questions.hint: The financial case deals with affordability and funding.

questions.prompt: A planning team has costed a new IT system using only the most favourable assumptions. Which concept should the team apply?

options.text: Optimism bias adjustments, for the tendency to underestimate costs
Discounting, to bring all future costs down to nothing in today's terms
Sensitivity analysis, to remove the uncertain figures from the appraisal
Distributional analysis, to share the costs fairly between groups

questions.hint: Optimism bias is addressed through explicit adjustments.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of discounting in appraisal?

options.text: To reduce the cost of a project in the department's budget lines
To apply a reduction in price for suppliers who bid early
To exclude benefits that fall more than five years in the future
To convert costs and benefits arising at different times into comparable present values

questions.hint: Discounting allows comparison across time.

questions.prompt: What does the economic case primarily do?

options.text: Sets out how the project will be governed and how risks will be managed
Compares options to show which offers best value for money to society
Explains the case for change and how it fits government objectives
Shows whether a viable deal with suppliers can be agreed

questions.hint: The economic case assesses value for money across options.

questions.prompt: A proposal's benefits depend heavily on one uncertain assumption. How should the appraisal handle this?

options.text: Drop the assumption and present the result as certain
Use the most optimistic value, to be consistent with the strategic case
Leave the uncertainty to the minister to resolve when approving
Use sensitivity analysis to test how results change if it is wrong

questions.hint: Sensitivity analysis tests the robustness of results.

questions.prompt: Which statement about the scope of the Green Book is correct?

options.text: It applies only to large capital projects above a high cost threshold
It applies only to local government, which follows its own rules
It covers appraisal and evaluation across central government
It sets the pay and grading structure for civil servants

questions.hint: The Green Book guides appraisal and evaluation across central government.

questions.prompt: What is the management case concerned with?

options.text: Whether the proposal can be delivered, including governance and risks
Whether the proposal fits the department's overall strategy and priorities
Whether the proposal is affordable within the department's budget
Whether suppliers are likely to bid and at what price

questions.hint: The management case concerns deliverability.

items.title: L13: Working with local authorities: funding and new burdens
items.source: Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government, New Burdens Doctrine guidance; Local Government Act 1972 section 151; Local Government Finance Act 1992
items.body: Local authorities are democratically elected bodies with their own powers, funding and accountability to local voters. They are not arms of central government, though they deliver many national policies, such as social care, planning, housing and waste. Central government influences them through legislation that gives them duties and powers, through grants and funding rules, through guidance, and, where necessary, through statutory intervention powers. It cannot direct their day-to-day operations. Funding comes from several sources: council tax set locally within referendum limits, business rates, government grants, and fees and charges. Some grants are ring-fenced, meaning they must be spent on a stated purpose, while others are unringfenced so councils decide how to use them. The new burdens doctrine requires central government to assess and, where it is net additional, fully fund the costs to local authorities of any new duties, powers or requirements it places on them. Departments consider the doctrine early when they plan new policy. Every council must appoint a chief financial officer, known as the section 151 officer after the law that requires it, with responsibility for the proper administration of the council's financial affairs, and who can issue a report if the council is likely to act unlawfully or spend more than it has. Officials working with local authorities should treat them as partners, consult them on new requirements, be clear about what is expected, avoid duplicate data requests, and remember that councils must balance their budgets and are accountable locally. Ministers can intervene in failing councils, for example by appointing commissioners, but only through legal powers and normally as a last resort.

questions.prompt: A department plans a new statutory duty requiring councils to publish a new data return. What should officials check first?

options.text: Whether the new burdens doctrine applies, so the net additional cost is assessed and funded
Whether councils can be required to meet the cost from their own reserves
Whether the duty can be imposed without consulting any council beforehand
Whether the Treasury will let the department pass the duty to a charity

questions.hint: The doctrine requires net new costs to be assessed early.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes a local authority's relationship with central government?

options.text: A government department that carries out ministers' instructions locally
A separate elected body, answerable to local voters
An executive agency of the department that sponsors local government
A non-departmental public body sponsored by the Treasury

questions.hint: Councils have their own democratic mandate.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between ring-fenced and unringfenced grants?

options.text: Ring-fenced grants must be repaid at year end, while unringfenced grants need not be
Ring-fenced grants are paid by the Treasury, while unringfenced grants come from the Cabinet Office
Ring-fenced grants may be spent only on capital, while unringfenced grants are for resource
Ring-fenced money must be spent on a stated purpose; unringfenced money need not

questions.hint: Ring-fencing restricts how a grant may be used.

questions.prompt: A section 151 officer believes a council is about to set an unlawful budget. What may they do?

options.text: Report it to the minister, who then decides whether the council may proceed
Cancel the budget on their own authority until it is made lawful
Issue a formal report to the council setting out the concern
Wait until the year-end accounts are prepared and then qualify them

questions.hint: The section 151 officer has a statutory role in warning the council.

questions.prompt: How can a minister intervene in a failing council?

options.text: By instructing council staff directly, since they are paid with government grant
By removing councillors at will where the minister thinks performance is poor
By setting the council tax rate for the area until performance improves
Through statutory powers such as appointing commissioners, as a last resort

questions.hint: Intervention needs a legal power and is normally a last resort.

questions.prompt: A department wants information from every council for a new scheme. How should officials approach it?

options.text: Issue it at short notice and expect it to be answered immediately
Ask each council in a different format to suit its own systems
Consult on the request, avoid duplicate returns and make the purpose clear
Make it a condition of grant without discussing it, so all councils comply

questions.hint: Good practice reduces burdens and respects councils' accountability.

questions.prompt: Where does most council funding come from?

options.text: Almost entirely government grants, set each year through the Supply Estimate process
A mix of council tax, business rates, government grants, and fees and charges
Almost entirely council tax, which councils set without any limits
The Treasury's annual allocation, topped up by the National Audit Office

questions.hint: Councils have several funding sources.

questions.prompt: Who decides how a council spends its unringfenced grant?

options.text: The council, through its elected members and officers
The department that paid the grant, using conditions attached to it
The Treasury, which approves each council's spending plans
The National Audit Office, which audits council spending each year

questions.hint: Unringfenced grants give the council discretion.

items.title: L13: Common frameworks and the UK internal market
items.source: UK Internal Market Act 2020; Cabinet Office, Common Frameworks guidance; Office for the Internal Market (Competition and Markets Authority)
items.body: When the UK left the European Union, many powers in devolved areas such as agriculture, the environment and food standards returned from EU law. To avoid unmanaged differences across the UK, the UK Government and the devolved governments agreed common frameworks. A common framework is an agreed approach to a policy area where regulatory consistency matters. It sets out how the governments will work together, share information, take decisions and manage differences, and it is developed by officials and agreed by ministers. Common frameworks respect devolution: they are not imposed by the UK Government and do not remove devolved powers, though governments commit to following the process and to discuss before diverging. They also give a route for resolving disputes by escalating to ministers. Separately, the UK Internal Market Act 2020 sets rules to protect trade across the four nations. It applies two market access principles, mutual recognition, meaning goods that can be sold lawfully in one part of the UK can generally be sold in another, and non-discrimination, meaning regulations should not treat goods or services from elsewhere in the UK less favourably than local ones, with limited exceptions. The Office for the Internal Market, part of the Competition and Markets Authority, provides independent monitoring and advice on how the internal market is working. The Act applies even where a devolved government has regulated differently, and the devolved governments have argued that it limits their powers. Officials should understand both, since a policy that creates a difference in rules between nations can raise questions under the framework process and under the Act.

questions.prompt: A UK department proposes a new product standard in an area covered by a common framework. What should officials do?

options.text: Issue the standard and inform the devolved governments once it is in force
Seek approval for the standard from the Office for the Internal Market
Follow the framework's process: share proposals and discuss them with devolved governments first
Ask the Speaker to certify that the standard is within UK competence

questions.hint: Frameworks set out how governments cooperate and manage differences.

questions.prompt: What does the mutual recognition principle in the UK Internal Market Act mean in practice?

options.text: Each nation must adopt identical product standards for goods sold there
Goods lawfully sold in one part of the UK can generally be sold in all
Devolved governments must accept UK Government rulings on all matters
Businesses must gain separate approval for the goods in each nation

questions.hint: Mutual recognition lets lawfully sold goods circulate across the UK.

questions.prompt: Which statement about common frameworks is correct?

options.text: They are legal rules imposed by the UK Government on the devolved administrations
They are decisions of the Competition and Markets Authority binding on all nations
They are Acts made by the House of Lords for the devolved nations
They are agreed approaches developed jointly by the governments

questions.hint: Common frameworks are collaborative, not imposed.

questions.prompt: What is the role of the Office for the Internal Market?

options.text: To monitor and advise on how the UK internal market is working
To approve each new regulation before it takes effect in any nation
To represent the devolved governments in disputes with the UK Government
To set the UK's trade policy with countries outside the UK

questions.hint: It sits within the Competition and Markets Authority and gives advice.

questions.prompt: A devolved government introduces a rule on the sale of a product that differs from the rest of the UK. Which concern might arise?

options.text: Whether the rule has been approved by the Public Accounts Committee
Whether the rule has been audited by the NAO before introduction
Whether the rule engages the market access principles for goods sold from elsewhere in the UK
Whether the rule is exempt from judicial review as devolved legislation

questions.hint: The Act's principles may affect how the rule applies to goods from other nations.

questions.prompt: What does non-discrimination mean under the Internal Market Act?

options.text: Every business must be treated identically whatever its size and sector
Rules should not treat goods from elsewhere in the UK less favourably than local goods
Consumers in every nation must pay the same price for the same goods
All nations must set the same rates of tax on the same products

questions.hint: It prevents less favourable treatment of goods and services from other UK nations.

questions.prompt: Why might officials in a UK department need to think about both common frameworks and the Act?

options.text: Both are statutes that require departments to publish their business plans
Both control departmental budgets and are administered by the Treasury
Both apply only to local authorities and not to central departments
A rule that differs between nations may raise issues under both the framework process and the Act

questions.hint: The two sit together in managing divergence.

questions.prompt: If governments disagree within a common framework, what is the usual route?

options.text: Escalation through the agreed process to senior officials, then ministers
An application to the courts, which settle all disagreements between governments
A decision by the Prime Minister alone, which binds the devolved governments
A referral to the Speaker of the House of Commons for a ruling

questions.hint: Frameworks include escalation to ministers.

items.title: L13: Public inquiries and what officials must do
items.source: Inquiries Act 2005; Cabinet Office guidance on public inquiries; Inquiry Rules 2006
items.body: A statutory public inquiry is set up by a minister under the Inquiries Act 2005 to investigate events of serious public concern. The minister defines the terms of reference and appoints the chair, who must be independent of the government and impartial. Once set up, the inquiry is independent: the chair decides how it is run, who gives evidence and what is published, and ministers cannot direct its conclusions. The inquiry has legal powers to require people to give evidence and to produce documents, backed by criminal penalties for failing to comply, and it can take evidence on oath. It does not decide civil or criminal liability, though it can make findings of fact and criticise individuals and organisations. Government departments are often core participants, with legal representation, which gives them rights to see evidence and make submissions. Before a report is published, those criticised may receive a warning letter and an opportunity to respond. Departments owe a duty to cooperate and to disclose relevant documents, including those which are unhelpful, and they must preserve documents from the moment an inquiry is likely. Officials may be asked to give written or oral witness statements, which should be accurate, based on the records, and honest about what they do not recall. Legal advisers normally help to prepare but the evidence must be the witness's own. After the report, the government normally responds publicly, often with an action plan, and monitors progress. Inquiries can last years, so records and lessons should be kept in a way that can be found later. Handling an inquiry is a test of the Civil Service values of honesty, objectivity and integrity.

questions.prompt: A department asks the minister to tell the chair of a statutory inquiry what to conclude. What is the correct position?

options.text: The minister may direct the chair if the department gives a good reason
The department may tell the chair directly what the inquiry should conclude
The inquiry is independent, so ministers cannot direct its conclusions
The Cabinet Secretary must approve the conclusions before publication

questions.hint: A statutory inquiry's chair is independent of government.

questions.prompt: An official receives an inquiry request for documents that do not help the department. What should they do?

options.text: Provide the relevant documents, as the duty to cooperate requires
Withhold them if they would damage the department's case at the hearings
Provide only those that show the department's decisions in a good light
Ask the minister to decide which of the documents should be sent

questions.hint: Departments must disclose relevant documents, including unhelpful ones.

questions.prompt: When should a department start preserving documents in case of an inquiry?

options.text: Only when the inquiry has begun to take evidence from witnesses
As soon as an inquiry is likely, not only once it is formally announced
Only when a particular document is specifically requested by the inquiry
After the report has been published, once the recommendations are known

questions.hint: Early preservation prevents loss of evidence.

questions.prompt: Which powers does a statutory inquiry have?

options.text: To impose criminal sentences on those it finds responsible after hearing the evidence
To set government policy in the area it investigates once the hearings are over
To order the dismissal of any civil servants whom the report criticises
To require witnesses to give evidence and produce documents

questions.hint: It has coercive evidence powers but does not decide liability.

questions.prompt: An official is asked for a witness statement about events they only partly remember. What is the right approach?

options.text: Fill the gaps with what probably happened and state it as fact
Ask a colleague who remembers better to write it on their behalf
Decline to give a statement until the minister has agreed its content
Base it on the records and say clearly what they do not recall

questions.hint: Honesty about memory is essential.

questions.prompt: What does it mean that a department is a core participant in an inquiry?

options.text: It chairs the hearings and decides which witnesses are called
It has legal representation and rights to see evidence and make submissions
It chooses the other witnesses, within the terms of reference
It is exempt from the inquiry's powers to require documents

questions.hint: Core participants have extra procedural rights.

questions.prompt: Before an inquiry report that criticises an individual is published, what normally happens?

options.text: The minister approves the criticisms before the report is finalised
The individual is told only after the report is published
A warning letter gives them a chance to respond before publication
The criticisms are removed automatically if the person objects

questions.hint: Fairness requires notice of criticism.

questions.prompt: What does a public inquiry not decide?

options.text: Civil or criminal liability
Findings of fact about what happened and why
Recommendations for change in the area investigated
Which witnesses are called to give evidence

questions.hint: An inquiry finds facts and recommends but does not determine liability.

items.title: L13: The Carltona principle and delegating ministers' powers
items.source: Carltona Ltd v Commissioners of Works [1943] 2 All ER 560; Cabinet Manual; departmental schemes of delegation
items.body: Many statutes give a power to a Secretary of State, such as the power to make a decision on a licence or to make a payment. A minister cannot personally take every decision. Under the Carltona principle, named after a 1943 case, a decision taken by an official on behalf of a minister is in law the minister's decision, provided the official is of suitable seniority for the matter and the statute does not require the minister to act personally. This is why a decision letter signed by an official can bind the department and why the minister remains answerable to Parliament for it. The principle is a rule about authorisation within a department. It does not allow the power to be handed to a person or body outside the department unless the statute allows, and the more significant the decision, the more senior the official needs to be. Some decisions are reserved to ministers, such as those with major public impact, controversial cases or those where the law expressly requires personal decision. Departments set out delegations in schemes of delegation so that officials know what they may decide. An official who goes beyond their delegated authority risks the decision being unlawful. Officials taking decisions on behalf of a minister must act within the law, follow fair procedures, be able to explain their reasons and keep records. If a decision is likely to be controversial or novel, they should consider whether to refer it to the minister, even if technically delegated. The principle also explains why a minister may be held to account for the errors of officials even without personal knowledge, although in modern practice ministers tend to accept responsibility for policy and answer for operational matters in proportion to their involvement.

questions.prompt: An official of suitable seniority signs a licence decision under a power given by statute to the Secretary of State. What is the legal effect?

options.text: It is a separate decision of the official, with no legal link to the minister
It has no effect until the minister has countersigned the decision letter
It binds only the official's own team and not the department as a whole
It is treated in law as the Secretary of State's own decision

questions.hint: Under Carltona the official's act is the minister's act.

questions.prompt: A statute says a decision is to be made by the Secretary of State personally. What does this mean for delegation?

options.text: An official may make it if they are senior enough for the decision
Any official may make it once the minister has agreed by email
It cannot be delegated to an official under the Carltona principle
The Permanent Secretary may make it automatically in the minister's place

questions.hint: The principle does not apply where the law requires personal decision.

questions.prompt: A department wants to hand a statutory decision-making power to a private contractor for convenience. What is the problem?

options.text: The principle covers officials; handing a power outside needs statutory permission
There is no problem, since contractors are treated like civil servants for decisions
The contractor can decide, but only while the minister is away from the department
It is lawful so long as the contractor is cheaper than doing it in-house

questions.hint: Authority inside the department does not stretch to outsiders without legal authority.

questions.prompt: What does a scheme of delegation set out?

options.text: Which policies a minister has approved for the coming year
Which officials may take which decisions
How the department's budget is divided between its directorates
Which engagements the minister will attend in the coming month

questions.hint: Schemes record authority within the department.

questions.prompt: How does the seniority of the official relate to the significance of the decision?

options.text: Seniority is irrelevant provided the official has read the file
The more significant the decision, the more junior the official should be
Only ministers may take any decision that has a financial effect
The more significant the decision, the more senior the official

questions.hint: Suitable seniority is a condition of valid delegation.

questions.prompt: An EO is asked to make a novel and controversial decision that is within their delegation on paper. What should they do?

options.text: Consider referring it up, since it is novel and controversial
Decide it, because the delegation allows it and the file supports a decision
Delay the decision until somebody complains about the case
Ask the person affected to say what outcome they would accept

questions.hint: Delegation does not remove the need for judgement about referral.

questions.prompt: Why does a minister remain answerable to Parliament for a decision taken by an official under delegation?

options.text: The official is employed by the minister personally
Parliament appoints the officials who take such decisions
In law it is the minister's decision, taken for them
Ministers sign every decision letter before it is sent out

questions.hint: Ministerial accountability follows from the legal identity of the decision.

questions.prompt: What may happen if an official makes a decision beyond their delegated authority?

options.text: It is valid anyway, because the minister has the power
It risks being unlawful and open to challenge
It is valid if colleagues support the decision
It becomes lawful after twelve months if nobody challenges it

questions.hint: Acting beyond authority undermines legality.

items.title: L13: Senior responsible owners and project assurance
items.source: Cabinet Office, Government Functional Standard GovS 002: Project delivery; Government Major Projects Portfolio; Gateway review guidance
items.body: Government projects and programmes are led by a senior responsible owner (SRO), a named senior official who is personally accountable for delivering the intended outcomes and benefits. The SRO is not simply a project manager. They own the business case, appoint or work with the project director who manages day-to-day delivery, ensure governance is in place, manage key risks and stakeholders, and report to the department's board. The SRO should have the authority and capacity for the role, and an SRO who moves on mid-project creates a risk of lost continuity, so departments try to keep SROs in post through critical stages. Major projects are tracked in the Government Major Projects Portfolio and given a delivery confidence assessment, which is a rating on a five-point scale from red to green that indicates how likely it is that the project will be delivered on time, to budget and to the expected quality. Assurance is provided independently of the project team. Gateway reviews are short, independent reviews at key points, such as business justification, delivery strategy, investment decision, readiness for service and benefits realisation, which give the SRO and the department an honest view of the project's health. Reviewers report to the SRO and the findings are confidential to the department, though the overall ratings of major projects are published. Good practice is that projects are told honestly when they are failing, and that red ratings are acted upon, not hidden. Accounting officers may seek assurance from SROs and may ask for a direction if a minister insists on a project that they believe cannot be delivered.

questions.prompt: An SRO tells the board that the project manager is fully responsible for whether the benefits are achieved. What is wrong with this?

options.text: The SRO is personally accountable for outcomes and benefits
Nothing: the SRO is responsible only for the project's budget
Nothing: the project manager is the person who approves the business case
The SRO's accountability ends once the budget has been approved

questions.hint: SRO accountability for outcomes is personal.

questions.prompt: A major project receives a red delivery confidence rating. What is the right response?

options.text: Hide the rating from the board to avoid damaging confidence
Change the project's objectives so the rating improves on paper
Act on it by finding the causes and agreeing remedial action
Wait to see whether the rating changes at the next review

questions.hint: Red ratings should prompt action.

questions.prompt: What is a Gateway review?

options.text: A final audit by the NAO once the project is complete
A meeting of ministers to approve each phase of a project
A report prepared by the project team for the board each quarter
A short independent review at a key point that gives an honest view of the project's health

questions.hint: Gateway reviews are independent assurance at key points.

questions.prompt: Why is it a risk if an SRO is moved frequently during a project?

options.text: The SRO's pay is linked to the project and must be recalculated each time
Continuity and accountability are lost, weakening delivery
The project manager must be replaced whenever the SRO changes
Ministers must formally reapprove the project each time

questions.hint: Continuity of leadership matters.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a key duty of an SRO?

options.text: Owning the business case and making sure governance and risk management are in place
Writing every document in the project personally to ensure consistency
Taking over the role of the project director when delivery runs late
Signing off the Treasury's decisions about the project's funding

questions.hint: The SRO owns the business case and governance.

questions.prompt: An accounting officer doubts that a project backed by the minister can be delivered. Which standard does this concern?

options.text: Regularity
Propriety
Feasibility
Value for money

questions.hint: Deliverability is the feasibility standard.

questions.prompt: Who receives the confidential findings of a Gateway review?

options.text: The public, through the Government Major Projects Portfolio
The SRO and the department, to use in improving the project
Parliament, which receives each review report as a matter of course
The supplier delivering the project, so that it can respond

questions.hint: The report goes to the SRO; ratings of major projects are published separately.

questions.prompt: Why should assurance be independent of the project team?

options.text: So the project team never sees the findings and cannot dispute them
So the Treasury can take over any project that is rated amber
So the project is cheaper to run than an internal review would be
So the SRO gets an honest view, not one shaped by the team

questions.hint: Independence supports candour.

items.title: L13: Transparency publications and what departments release
items.source: GOV.UK, Government transparency data; Cabinet Office, Transparency and Open Data guidance; Local Government Transparency Code
items.body: Transparency is a feature of how modern government works, and departments publish many types of information proactively, without waiting to be asked under the Freedom of Information Act. Central government departments publish spending over £25,000 each month, giving the date, the supplier and what it was for, so that the public can see where money goes. They publish organisation charts showing senior posts and the salaries of senior officials above a set level, and information about the meetings of ministers and senior officials with external organisations, and ministers' gifts, hospitality and overseas travel, usually every quarter. Contracts and tender opportunities above set thresholds are published through the government's procurement services. Departments also publish annual reports and accounts, business plans, performance data and statistics, often on GOV.UK or data.gov.uk. Statistics are produced to professional standards under the Code of Practice for Statistics, overseen by the Office for Statistics Regulation, which is independent of ministers. Official statistics are released at set times announced in advance, with no early access except for strictly limited groups, so that they cannot be used for political advantage. Transparency has limits. Some information must be protected, for example personal data, commercially sensitive information, national security and legal advice, and releasing it could breach the law or harm interests. Officials should therefore plan what they publish, check it for personal data and accuracy, remove sensitive details by proper redaction rather than by covering text in a way that can be reversed, and make data easy to use. Over-disclosing by accident is a data breach and under-disclosing erodes trust.

questions.prompt: A team publishes monthly spend over £25,000, but one column includes individual claimants' names. What is the problem?

options.text: It discloses personal data that should have been removed before publication
It is fine, because transparency commitments override data protection duties
It breaches the rule that only monthly totals may be published
It breaches the Code of Practice for Statistics on release times

questions.hint: Proactive publication must still protect personal data.

questions.prompt: Why are official statistics released at pre-announced times?

options.text: To give ministers time to decide whether the figures should be published
To stop early access being used for political advantage
To let departments edit the figures before release if they are unflattering
Because statistics teams only have capacity to publish on certain days

questions.hint: Pre-announcement supports trustworthiness.

questions.prompt: Which body oversees the Code of Practice for Statistics?

options.text: The Cabinet Office Propriety and Ethics team
The National Audit Office
The Treasury's Chief Economist group
The Office for Statistics Regulation

questions.hint: The OSR is independent of ministers.

questions.prompt: An official hides a sensitive paragraph in a published PDF by covering it with a black box that sits on an editable layer. What is the issue?

options.text: There is no problem, because a black box is the approved redaction method
The paragraph should be shown in red text so readers know it is sensitive
The text can still be recovered; redaction must remove it permanently
The PDF becomes exempt from the Freedom of Information Act once marked

questions.hint: Inadequate redaction can disclose the hidden text.

questions.prompt: What do departments typically publish about ministers each quarter?

options.text: Private diaries for each day of the quarter
External meetings, gifts, hospitality and travel
Personal bank details, to show their finances are clean
Party membership records and donations received

questions.hint: These are the standard quarterly transparency returns.

questions.prompt: A department fails to publish its monthly spend data for one month. What is the likely concern?

options.text: It undermines transparency commitments and trust, so should be corrected promptly
It does not matter, since publication of monthly data is optional
The Treasury will withdraw the department's budget for the year
The NAO will take over publication of the department's data

questions.hint: Regular publication is a commitment, so gaps matter.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a legitimate limit on proactive transparency?

options.text: A wish to avoid criticism of the department's spending
The preference of the minister about what is published
The workload of the press office around publication dates
Duties to protect personal data, commercial sensitivity and national security

questions.hint: Legitimate limits protect legal and security interests.

questions.prompt: What is the main benefit of publishing information proactively?

options.text: It removes the need for any FOI exemptions to be considered
It makes the government's decisions final and not open to challenge
It lets the public scrutinise government without asking
It increases the department's budget for communications

questions.hint: Proactive release supports accountability.

items.title: L13: Evaluating policy: the Magenta Book and evidence
items.source: HM Treasury, The Magenta Book: Central Government Guidance on Evaluation; Evaluation Task Force; What Works Network
items.body: Evaluation is the systematic assessment of how a policy or programme was designed, delivered and what difference it made. The Magenta Book is HM Treasury's guidance on evaluation, a companion to the Green Book. Evaluation types include process evaluation, which looks at how a policy was implemented and what worked in delivery, impact evaluation, which asks what difference the policy made and whether outcomes can be attributed to it, and economic evaluation, which compares benefits and costs. Impact evaluation relies on a counterfactual, an estimate of what would have happened without the policy. The strongest designs include randomised controlled trials, in which people or places are randomly assigned to receive the policy or not, and quasi-experimental methods, which use statistical techniques to compare similar groups when randomisation is not possible. A before and after comparison alone is weak, because other factors may have changed during the period. Good evaluation is planned from the start of a policy, not added at the end, so that baseline data are collected, the design can be built into roll-out, for example through a staged pilot, and the evaluation questions are agreed. It should be proportionate to the importance and risk of the policy, independent enough to be credible, and open about limitations. Findings should be published, including where they are unwelcome, and used to improve decisions. Officials should resist the temptation to present positive findings selectively. The What Works Network is a set of centres that assess evidence on what is effective in areas such as education, crime and health. Learning from failure is part of the Civil Service's culture of honesty.

questions.prompt: A department introduces a scheme and compares claimant numbers before and after, noting a fall. Why is this weak evidence of impact?

options.text: Before and after comparisons are not permitted under the Magenta Book
The number of claimants can only be counted after a full year has passed
Other factors may have changed in the same period
A minister must approve any comparison before it counts as evidence

questions.hint: Without a counterfactual, other causes cannot be excluded.

questions.prompt: What is a counterfactual in evaluation?

options.text: An estimate of what would have happened without the policy
A statement that the policy has not achieved what it set out to do
A list of the costs the policy has imposed on other departments
A report on the policy sent to Parliament each year

questions.hint: Impact depends on comparing with what would otherwise have happened.

questions.prompt: Which evaluation design gives the strongest evidence of impact?

options.text: A case study of one area where the policy worked very well
A survey of satisfied users carried out by the delivery team
A comparison with the previous year's national figures
A randomised controlled trial

questions.hint: RCTs randomise to create comparable groups.

questions.prompt: When should evaluation be planned?

options.text: After five years, when enough data has built up for analysis
From the start, so baseline data are collected and roll-out can support comparison
Only if the policy appears to have failed in its early months
Once the minister has asked for it in a submission

questions.hint: Early planning makes good evaluation possible.

questions.prompt: An evaluation shows that a policy had no measurable effect. What should officials do?

options.text: Delay publication until the minister has agreed the findings
Present only the positive findings from the process evaluation
Report it honestly, publish it and use it to inform decisions
Commission another evaluation until one shows an effect

questions.hint: Honesty about unwelcome results matters.

questions.prompt: What does a process evaluation examine?

options.text: How the policy was implemented and what worked in delivery
Whether the policy was popular with the main opposition party
Whether the policy saved money for the Treasury overall
Whether the policy was lawful at the time it was introduced

questions.hint: Process evaluation looks at delivery.

questions.prompt: Why might a staged pilot support evaluation?

options.text: It guarantees the policy will succeed when it is rolled out nationally
It removes the need to collect any baseline data beforehand
It makes the national policy cheaper than a full launch
It lets some areas go first, creating a comparison group

questions.hint: Staged roll-outs create comparison groups.

questions.prompt: What is the role of the What Works Network?

options.text: To decide government policy in the areas of education, crime and health
To assess and share evidence on what is effective in fields such as education and crime
To audit the accounts of departments working in those fields
To set pay and grading for civil servants in those fields

questions.hint: The network supports evidence-based decisions.

items.title: L13: Cross-government spend controls
items.source: Cabinet Office, Controls guidance and Spend Controls process; HM Treasury, Managing Public Money (delegated authorities)
items.body: In addition to Treasury approval, the Cabinet Office operates controls over particular categories of spending in which central co-ordination can improve value and consistency. Departments usually need approval before committing to spend above set thresholds on digital and technology, marketing and advertising, consultancy and professional services, property, and some recruitment and staffing matters. The aim is to challenge duplication, apply common standards, use central buying agreements, and ensure value for money. The thresholds and categories change over time and vary by department, so officials should check current guidance and ask their finance or commercial team rather than assume. The controls work alongside, not in place of, the department's own internal approvals. A typical process is that a team prepares a short case explaining the need, options, costs, benefits and alternatives such as reuse of existing systems, the department's internal governance approves it, and it is then submitted to the relevant control team. Approval can be given with conditions, or refused, or the proposal may be asked to resubmit. Spending commitments made without the required approval can be irregular and may need to be reported by the accounting officer. Officials should build the time for approval into project plans, because late applications can delay delivery, and should not split contracts to avoid the thresholds. The controls are also a source of data and expertise, helping government to spot patterns, share lessons, and negotiate better terms with large suppliers. Spend controls are different from the Treasury's delegated limits, which cover a department's overall authority, and from the department's own limits for individual budget holders.

questions.prompt: A team plans to hire consultants for a significant sum. What should it do before signing a contract?

options.text: Check whether the consultancy controls apply and seek approval first if over the threshold
Sign the contract and apply for approval afterwards to save time
Split the work into smaller contracts so each falls under the threshold
Ask the supplier to confirm whether approval is needed

questions.hint: Controls require approval before commitment.

questions.prompt: Why is it wrong to split a contract to avoid a control threshold?

options.text: It makes procurement more expensive without improving anything
It defeats the control and may make the spending irregular
It is acceptable if the parts are completed on different days
It breaches data protection law as well as the controls

questions.hint: Splitting is a form of avoidance.

questions.prompt: What is the main aim of Cabinet Office spend controls?

options.text: To replace the department's own internal approvals with central ones
To cut spending on all projects by a fixed percentage each year
To reward the departments that spend the most with larger budgets
To challenge duplication and secure value for money

questions.hint: Controls support value and consistency.

questions.prompt: Thresholds for controls change over time. What is the best approach?

options.text: Rely on the thresholds that applied when the project started
Assume they apply only to the largest departments
Check current guidance and ask the finance team
Ask the supplier which thresholds apply to the contract

questions.hint: Thresholds change, so check.

questions.prompt: A request for approval is refused with a recommendation to reuse an existing system. What is the sensible response?

options.text: Go ahead anyway, since the control team cannot stop a department
Challenge the control team's authority to review the case
Cancel the whole programme because the first proposal was refused
Consider the reuse option seriously and resubmit if the case for new spend is stronger

questions.hint: Controls challenge duplication.

questions.prompt: How should a project plan handle the approval process?

options.text: Build in time for approval, as late applications delay delivery
Leave it until the contract is ready to sign, to avoid duplication
Ignore it, because approval is nearly always automatic
Hand it to the supplier, who can apply on the department's behalf

questions.hint: Early planning avoids delays.

questions.prompt: What may happen if a commitment is made without required approval?

options.text: The Treasury will meet the cost automatically as a central charge
The minister is required to resign for a breach of the controls
The spending may be irregular and the accounting officer may have to report it
The supplier must refund the value of the contract in full

questions.hint: Unapproved commitments are an irregularity risk.

questions.prompt: How do Cabinet Office spend controls differ from a budget holder's delegated limit?

options.text: They replace the budget holder's limit for those categories
They are an extra check on particular categories, separate from the individual limit
They are the same as the limit, under a different name
They apply only to ministers and not to officials

questions.hint: Controls sit alongside delegations.

items.title: L13: Operational resilience and continuity planning
items.source: Cabinet Office, Government Functional Standard GovS 008: Security (resilience); ISO 22301 Business continuity management; National Cyber Security Centre guidance
items.body: Departments depend on services that must keep running when something goes wrong: a payments system, a contact centre, a registration service or a border system. Operational resilience is the ability to prevent, adapt to, respond to and recover from disruption while continuing to deliver critical services. Planning starts by identifying the critical functions and the people, premises, technology and suppliers they depend on. A business impact analysis shows how loss of each function affects outcomes over time, and identifies the maximum tolerable period of disruption, the longest a function can be unavailable before the impact becomes unacceptable. A business continuity plan then sets out how the function will carry on or be restored: alternative locations, manual workarounds, recovery priorities, communication routes, and the roles and decision rights of the people involved, together with current contact details. Dependencies on a single supplier are a common weakness, so plans should consider supplier failure and alternative options. Plans that exist only on paper are not enough: they should be tested through exercises, ranging from desk-top walkthroughs to live simulations, because gaps in roles, contacts and assumptions usually appear only when people try to use them. Lessons are recorded and the plan updated after every exercise, incident or major change. Cyber attacks are one of the most significant risks. Departments follow guidance from the National Cyber Security Centre, report serious incidents promptly, and plan how to operate with systems unavailable. The Permanent Secretary is accountable for the department's resilience and delegates specific responsibilities to senior officials and the board, which reviews risks regularly. Officials in operational teams should know their own part of the plan.

questions.prompt: A team wants to know which of its services most urgently need a recovery plan. Which exercise helps most?

options.text: A business impact analysis, showing the effect of losing each function
A risk register entry that lists the minister's priorities for the year
A benefits realisation plan setting out when each service will repay its cost
A framework document that sets out a sponsored body's recovery duties

questions.hint: A business impact analysis identifies which functions matter most and how quickly.

questions.prompt: Why test a continuity plan through an exercise rather than only reviewing it on paper?

options.text: Exercises are required by law before a plan can be approved
A paper review cannot be accepted by auditors in any circumstances
Exercises make it unnecessary to update the plan afterwards
Gaps in roles, contacts and dependencies often appear only when people try to use it

questions.hint: Exercises reveal practical weaknesses.

questions.prompt: A critical service depends on a single IT supplier. What should continuity planning include?

options.text: A clause making the minister personally liable if the supplier fails
A decision to leave the supplier off the risk register because it is contracted
An assessment of what happens if the supplier fails, with options for keeping the service going
A request that the supplier hold the department's plan on its own systems

questions.hint: Supplier dependency is a common weakness.

questions.prompt: Which element makes a continuity plan usable in a real incident?

options.text: A long narrative description of the department's history and purpose
Clear roles, current contact details and a tested way to reach staff
A statement from the minister endorsing the plan, without operational detail
A detailed forecast of the budget for the year of the incident

questions.hint: A usable plan names who does what and how to reach them.

questions.prompt: Who is accountable for a department's operational resilience?

options.text: The Permanent Secretary, delegating to senior officials
The Cabinet Office, which runs continuity for every department
The Prime Minister's office, which approves each department's plan
The Civil Contingencies Secretariat, as owner of every plan

questions.hint: The Permanent Secretary is accountable and delegates.

questions.prompt: A department suffers a ransomware attack on its payment system. What should the continuity response include?

options.text: Paying the ransom quickly to restore service, with the minister's agreement
Deleting affected files to stop the attack spreading to other departments
Following the incident plan: contain, report to security teams and the NCSC, prioritise critical payments
Waiting until the system is fully restored before telling anyone outside the team

questions.hint: Prompt reporting and a prepared plan limit the harm.

questions.prompt: How often should a continuity plan be reviewed?

options.text: Only when the Public Accounts Committee asks for it
Once, when it is first written, since the risks do not change
Every ten years, in line with records retention rules
Regularly, and after any incident, exercise or major change in the service or supplier

questions.hint: Plans must be kept up to date.

questions.prompt: What does the maximum tolerable period of disruption describe?

options.text: The longest a minister may remain in post without a reshuffle
The longest a function can be unavailable before the impact is unacceptable
The time within which an FOI request must be answered during an incident
The period for which the department's budget is set under the Spending Review

questions.hint: It sets recovery priorities.
